steps.title: Construct PyTorch input tensors with compatible shapes and dtypes

blocks.text: Keep the order features and targets aligned, with a separate representation contract for each.

Import torch, then construct each supplied NumPy array's tensor with torch.from_numpy(array). For each tensor, explicitly apply tensor.to(dtype=declared_dtype) and inspect tensor.shape and tensor.dtype. Check row correspondence; do not infer the target representation from the feature dtype. Before returning the aligned tuple, assert each declared axis length and the shared batch length.
Test valid, boundary and failure fixtures with assert predicates. A false predicate raises AssertionError in ordinary non-optimized execution.

These fixtures already supply corresponding observation order. Equal batch lengths alone do not prove that each feature row belongs to its target; verify that correspondence using the supplied observation identifiers or pairing reference.

blocks.code:
import torch

def prepare(features_array, targets_array, feature_dtype, target_dtype,
            feature_shape, target_shape):
    features = torch.from_numpy(features_array).to(dtype=feature_dtype)
    targets = torch.from_numpy(targets_array).to(dtype=target_dtype)
    assert features.shape == feature_shape
    assert targets.shape == target_shape
    assert features.shape[0] == targets.shape[0]
    assert features.dtype == feature_dtype
    assert targets.dtype == target_dtype
    return features, targets

# Fixtures supply corresponding observation order and separate declared dtypes.
# Run accepted and boundary pairs; the mismatched-target fixture must fail.
for fixture in accepted_and_boundary_fixtures:
    features, targets = prepare(**fixture)
try:
    prepare(**three_target_failure_fixture)
except AssertionError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("Expected the alignment check to reject this fixture")

Build a dataset and minibatch loader

blocks.text: The dataset defines a paired observation; the loader groups those pairs under your declared policy.

Implement a map-style Dataset with __len__ reporting sample count and __getitem__(index) retrieving its paired feature/target item. When observations are lists, use the same index for features and targets and return that pair as a tuple. Construct DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=declared_size, shuffle=declared_order_policy) and iterate for features, targets in loader.

Minibatches group observation items; each item's feature/target relationship stays intact. Set DataLoader(..., drop_last=True) to discard the last incomplete batch, or drop_last=False (the default) to retain it with fewer samples than batch_size; test the observed batch boundaries against that explicit choice. Test valid, boundary and failure fixtures with assert predicates. A false predicate raises AssertionError in ordinary non-optimized execution.
Here, `feature_observations` and `target_observations` are lists whose individual items are tensors, so the loader stacks them into minibatch tensors.

blocks.text: For five indexed observations and batch_size 2, a fixture with drop_last=False retains batches of sizes 2, 2 and 1. With drop_last=True, it retains two complete batches and discards the incomplete final batch. Retrieve each feature and target from the same observation index in __getitem__, and return them together. Test the batch boundaries and observed pairings under the declared shuffle policy rather than assuming a loader output's first position still corresponds to the source's first row. Also check __len__ against the sample count.
The choice about the incomplete batch must appear in the fixture expectations, because counting three batches of size two would invent an observation.

Define a neural network with task-compatible layers and activations

blocks.text: Build from the input width to the task output contract, checking every layer boundary.

After importing torch.nn as nn, subclass nn.Module. Call super().__init__(), register layers as attributes and define forward(self, x). nn.Linear(in_features, out_features) maps each input feature vector to out_features outputs using learned weights and bias, preserving the leading minibatch dimension. nn.ReLU applies max(0, x) elementwise and introduces a nonlinearity between linear layers.

In nn.Sequential, modules run in the declared order. Each output width must match the next input width. Set the final layer width and activation to the supplied output task contract and verify the resulting output shape with a fixture batch.

steps.title: Compute neural-network gradients with automatic differentiation

blocks.text: Use the chain-rule reference to check autograd, not just the existence of a gradient.

Autograd builds a computation graph from tensor operations, then applies the chain rule to differentiate its scalar output. Mark trainable leaves with requires_grad=True. Form the supplied scalar loss and call loss.backward(); inspect .grad on each leaf parameter. Clear old gradients before a fresh reference comparison: backward accumulates into .grad.

For a linear batch Z = XW + b with scalar-loss derivative D = ∂L/∂Z, the chain rule yields ∂L/∂W = X.T @ D and ∂L/∂b = D.sum(axis=0), with any loss reduction already included in D. Compare the computed gradients to the matrix-shaped chain-rule reference with explicit relative and absolute tolerances. Test valid, boundary and failure fixtures with assert predicates. A false predicate raises AssertionError in ordinary non-optimized execution.

blocks.code:
import torch

W = supplied_W.clone().requires_grad_(True)
b = supplied_b.clone().requires_grad_(True)
W.grad = None
b.grad = None
Z = X @ W + b
loss = supplied_scalar_loss(Z, targets)
loss.backward()
# D is the supplied scalar-loss derivative, including its reduction.
reference_W = X.T @ D
reference_b = D.sum(dim=0)
assert W.grad.shape == reference_W.shape
assert b.grad.shape == reference_b.shape
assert torch.allclose(W.grad, reference_W, rtol=rtol, atol=atol)
assert torch.allclose(b.grad, reference_b, rtol=rtol, atol=atol)

Choose a task-compatible training loss

blocks.text: Choose the output and target contract before choosing the scalar objective.

The scalar objective compares outputs with their corresponding targets. First establish the loss's input contract. CrossEntropyLoss expects unnormalized class logits; for class-index targets, logits have shape (N, C), targets have shape (N,) with dtype long and values in [0, C). For MSELoss, inputs and targets must share a shape. Mean reduction averages the squared elementwise differences.

blocks.code:
from torch import nn

# Class indices: raw logits (N, C), long targets (N,), indices in [0, C).
class_loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(class_logits, class_indices)
# Numerical targets: same shape as outputs.
regression_loss = nn.MSELoss(reduction="mean")(outputs, numeric_targets)
# Binary targets: same shape, values in [0, 1], raw logits as inputs.
binary_loss = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss(reduction="mean")(binary_logits, binary_targets)

mse_D = 2 * (outputs - numeric_targets) / outputs.numel()
binary_D = (binary_logits.sigmoid() - binary_targets) / binary_logits.numel()
class_D = (class_logits.softmax(dim=1) - one_hot_targets) / class_logits.shape[0]

steps.title: Choose a task-compatible training loss

blocks.text: BCEWithLogitsLoss combines sigmoid and binary cross-entropy for logits and same-shaped targets in [0, 1], rather than expecting already-sigmoid-transformed inputs. For mean squared error over M output elements, the loss derivative with respect to an output is 2 × (output−target)/M, so its sign points toward increasing loss as the output moves away from the target. For unweighted mean binary cross-entropy with logits over M elements, the logit derivative is (sigmoid(logit)−target)/M; this distinguishes the probability representation from the raw logit.

For mean class-index cross-entropy without weighting, the derivative per sample logit is (softmax probability−one-hot target)/N, so output width, target identity and reduction affect the gradient reference.

steps.title: Choose a task-compatible training loss

blocks.text: For an unweighted mean squared-error fixture with outputs [2, 4] and targets [1, 2], the loss is (1²+2²)/2 = 2.5 and output derivatives are [1, 2]. For a binary-logit fixture with one logit 0 and target 1, sigmoid(0)=0.5, so the supplied mean-logit derivative is −0.5. For target 1, decreasing the logit increases loss, while increasing it decreases loss. For a class-index task with three classes, verify logits width 3 and long target indices in [0, 3); use the stated softmax-minus-one-hot reference with its sample-count reduction.
These are distinct output contracts, not interchangeable wrappers around arbitrary tensors.

Configure a baseline optimizer and learning rate

blocks.text: Give plain SGD the trainable parameters and verify one current-gradient update.

Pass the model's trainable parameters to torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=declared_learning_rate). For plain SGD without momentum, weight decay or other modifications, the parameter update is parameter_new = parameter_old − learning_rate × gradient. Apply the current update in order: optimizer.zero_grad() clears old gradients, loss.backward() computes gradients, and optimizer.step() updates parameters.

Check one deterministic fixture update against the declared plain-SGD equation, without extending that rule to every optimizer. Test valid, boundary and failure fixtures with assert predicates. A false predicate raises AssertionError in ordinary non-optimized execution.

before.code:
import torch
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate)
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss = loss_fn(model(features), targets)
loss.backward()
before = [p.detach().clone() for p in model.parameters()]
gradients = [p.grad.detach().clone() for p in model.parameters()]

after.code:
optimizer.step()
for p, old, gradient in zip(model.parameters(), before, gradients):
    expected = old - learning_rate * gradient
    assert torch.allclose(p.detach(), expected, rtol=rtol, atol=atol)

Retain the before and after values and compare their difference with the reference under declared tolerances. Initialize the optimizer with model.parameters() so it acts on the supplied trainable model parameters.

A fixture that calls backward but never step would produce a gradient without this parameter update. Keep the plain-SGD restrictions visible so this arithmetic is not mistaken for the update rule of every optimizer.

steps.title: Implement the minibatch forward, backward and optimizer-step loop

blocks.text: Each minibatch needs its own forward pass, fresh gradient and parameter update.

Iterate for features, targets in loader inside each declared epoch, compute predictions with model(features), then loss_fn(predictions, targets). For every minibatch, use optimizer.zero_grad(), loss.backward() and optimizer.step() in order; the update must use that minibatch's current gradient. Collect scalar evidence with loss.item(). Keep batch counts in the epoch summary, including an incomplete batch rather than silently treating it as full.

Test valid, boundary and failure fixtures with assert predicates. A false predicate raises AssertionError in ordinary non-optimized execution. For a plain-SGD fixture, retain parameter values before the step and assert parameter_after − parameter_before agrees with −learning_rate × current_gradient under tolerance.

blocks.code:
import torch

for epoch in range(declared_epochs):
    batch_records = []
    for features, targets in loader:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        predictions = model(features)
        loss = loss_fn(predictions, targets)
        loss.backward()
        before = [p.detach().clone() for p in model.parameters()]
        gradients = [p.grad.detach().clone() for p in model.parameters()]
        optimizer.step()
        # This fixture uses plain SGD only.
        for p, old, gradient in zip(model.parameters(), before, gradients):
            assert torch.allclose(p.detach() - old, -learning_rate * gradient,
                                  rtol=rtol, atol=atol)
        batch_records.append((loss.item(), features.shape[0]))

steps.title: Implement the minibatch forward, backward and optimizer-step loop

blocks.text: With five observations and retained batches of sizes 2, 2 and 1, compute model outputs and loss for each aligned feature/target pair. For every minibatch, zero gradients, backpropagate that batch's loss and apply the optimizer step. Collect scalar loss.item() values with batch counts, so an epoch summary does not pretend all batches contain two observations. In the deterministic plain-SGD fixture, retain the pre-step parameter and compare its observed change with −learning_rate × current_gradient under tolerance. Test the loop's supplied valid, boundary and failure cases.
The repeated sequence is what links each batch to its intended current gradient, rather than using an accumulated leftover from another batch.

Apply correct neural-network training and evaluation modes

blocks.text: Validation needs both the right layer behavior and disabled gradient recording.

Use model.train() during parameter training and model.eval() during validation; the mode changes behavior of layers such as dropout and batch normalization. Wrap validation prediction in with torch.no_grad(): to disable graph recording and avoid building gradients for validation. Separate the two controls: eval changes relevant layer behavior; no_grad controls gradient recording.

left.code:
import torch
from torch import nn
layer = nn.Dropout(p=declared_dropout_probability)
layer.train()
with torch.no_grad():
    training_output = layer(x)
# no_grad does not switch dropout behavior.
assert torch.all((training_output == 0) |
                 (training_output == x / (1 - layer.p)))

right.code:
layer.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    evaluation_output = layer(x)
assert torch.equal(evaluation_output, x)
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    validation_predictions = model(validation_features)
# Forward only: no optimizer.step().
model.train()

blocks.takeaway: Layer mode and graph recording are separate.

steps.title: Stop training using validation behavior without consulting the protected test

blocks.text: Declare the validation stopping rule before training, and preserve the accepted best weights.

Before training, declare the validation quantity, direction, minimum improvement and patience. Patience counts consecutive epochs lacking sufficient improvement. For a minimized validation quantity, reset the non-improvement counter only when current < best − min_delta; otherwise increment it and stop when the declared patience is exhausted. Here, best is the validation value at the most recent checkpoint accepted under min_delta, not necessarily the lowest observed value. Retain that accepted checkpoint’s model weights not automatically the last epoch’s weights.

blocks.code:
from copy import deepcopy

best = float("inf")
non_improvements = 0
epoch = 0
best_state = None
while epoch < maximum_epochs:
    train_one_epoch()
    current = validation_loss_forward_only()
    epoch += 1
    if current < best - min_delta:
        best = current
        non_improvements = 0
        best_state = deepcopy(model.state_dict())
    else:
        non_improvements += 1
        if non_improvements >= patience:
            break
model.load_state_dict(best_state)
# No protected-test observations enter this controller.

steps.title: Stop training using validation behavior without consulting the protected test

blocks.text: A state_dict refers to live parameter values, so preserve a best-epoch state with a deep copy or a saved state file before later updates alter the model. Do not use protected test observations to fit preprocessing, choose a model or tune its settings; doing so leaks information into the chosen system. Implement the controller as a while loop bounded by maximum epochs and the non-improvement rule; update best loss/checkpoint inside the improvement branch and use break when patience is exhausted.

blocks.text: In the supplied fixture, minimized validation values are 0.50, 0.44, 0.43 and 0.45, with min_delta 0.02 and patience 2. The move from 0.50 to 0.44 is sufficient improvement and resets the counter. The value 0.43 does not satisfy 0.43 < 0.44−0.02, so the counter becomes one; 0.45 makes it two and exhausts patience. The lowest observed value is 0.43, but the best checkpoint accepted under min_delta is the one at 0.44. Retain the 0.44 checkpoint’s weights, preserving them by deep copy or a saved state file.

Diagnose training memory exhaustion

blocks.text: Locate the failure among simultaneous live allocations before choosing one correction.

Distinguish the CUDA readings: memory_allocated measures tensor-occupied memory, while memory_reserved includes caching-allocator storage. Inspect the workload’s peak allocated and reserved memory and the point of failure before attributing the failure to the input batch alone. Retaining tensors attached to computation graphs can retain graph memory; use detached/scalar diagnostic values when gradients through those saved values are not needed.

empty_cache releases unused cache for other uses, not storage still occupied by live tensors. Change one supported factor, such as reducing minibatch size or removing an unnecessary retained graph reference, and verify completion and the measured peak on the same bounded workload. Account for each parameter, gradient, activation and batch matrix as element_count × element_width, then sum simultaneously live allocations rather than only the input matrix.

tiles.title: Profile training compute and data-loading bottlenecks / Choose CPU or GPU capacity for a bounded training workload

steps.title: Profile training compute and data-loading bottlenecks

blocks.text: Locate the slow region, then verify any change with matched, unprofiled timing.

Use a PyTorch profiler context around the measured computation. Label data-loading and model-computation regions with record_function. Inspect key_averages().table(...) or the trace to attribute elapsed operator and labeled-region work to the observed bottleneck. Warm up before comparing steady-state execution. For the final timing comparison, run unprofiled to remove profiler overhead.

CUDA work is asynchronous, so CPU clock timings require synchronization at the measurement boundaries to include completed accelerator work. Change one supported bottleneck factor and remeasure the same bounded workload. A code edit alone does not demonstrate improvement. Inspect CPU and memory measurements and running process state during the profiled interval, using docker stats and docker top for a containerized run, to distinguish resource limits from stage timing evidence.

left.code:
import torch
from torch.profiler import profile, record_function
warm_up_workload()
with profile(activities=declared_activities) as prof:
    with record_function("data_loading"):
        features, targets = next(iterator)
    with record_function("model_computation"):
        run_bounded_model_computation(features, targets)
inspect_profile(prof.key_averages().table())
# During a containerized interval, inspect docker stats and docker top.

right.code:
# Final comparison: same workload, no profiler overhead.
apply_one_supported_bottleneck_change()
warm_up_workload()

steps.title: Task specific pretrained weight fine tuning

blocks.text: Keep the pretrained baseline mapping separate from the new task head mapping.

For the bounded ViT image-classification adaptation, import torch, nn from torch, and AutoImageProcessor, ViTForImageClassification, TrainingArguments and Trainer from transformers. Load the supplied compatible checkpoint with ViTForImageClassification.from_pretrained(checkpoint). Retain its original label mapping for the pretrained baseline before replacing the task head. Load the matching processor with AutoImageProcessor.from_pretrained(checkpoint). Calling that processor on images with return_tensors="pt" produces pixel_values; passing the resulting inputs as keyword arguments to the model yields logits through its .logits attribute. Use this same checkpoint processor for training and validation images rather than an unrelated representation.

With the supplied preprocessed datasets and image collator, construct TrainingArguments with the declared output_dir, num_train_epochs, per_device_train_batch_size and learning_rate. Set eval_strategy="epoch" and remove_unused_columns=False. Construct Trainer with model, args, train_dataset, eval_dataset=validation_dataset, data_collator and processing_class=processor. Its train method executes the bounded supervised adaptation.

left.code:
import torch
from torch import nn
from transformers import AutoImageProcessor, ViTForImageClassification
from transformers import TrainingArguments, Trainer
model = ViTForImageClassification.from_pretrained(checkpoint)
processor = AutoImageProcessor.from_pretrained(checkpoint)
original_id2label = dict(model.config.id2label)
original_label2id = dict(model.config.label2id)
inputs = processor(images, return_tensors="pt")
frozen_baseline_logits = model(**inputs).logits
# Retain baseline outputs on the same validation cohort.

right.code:
for parameter in model.parameters():
    parameter.requires_grad = False
model.classifier = nn.Linear(model.config.hidden_size, num_labels)
model.num_labels = model.config.num_labels = num_labels
model.config.id2label = id2label
model.config.label2id = label2id
args = TrainingArguments(output_dir=output_dir, num_train_epochs=epochs,
    per_device_train_batch_size=batch_size, learning_rate=learning_rate,
    eval_strategy="epoch", remove_unused_columns=False)
trainer = Trainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=train_dataset,
    eval_dataset=validation_dataset, data_collator=data_collator,
    processing_class=processor)
trainer.train()
